Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Asher Hernandez was a seasoned prosecutor with over seven years of experience in the courtroom. He had seen it all - or so he thought. That fateful evening three years ago changed everything. Asher was attending a networking event at a crowded restaurant in downtown Manhattan when a bomb exploded, ripping through the room and leaving chaos in its wake. The sound still echoes in his mind like it happened yesterday. As he tries to recount that night's events, Asher finds himself struggling to piece together a coherent story. Fragments of memories linger - the smell of smoke and cheap perfume, the feeling of being knocked off balance, the screams for help. However, whenever he attempts to assemble these fragments into a clear narrative, his mind goes blank. He feels like an outsider looking in on someone else's tragedy. These disjointed memories haunt Asher, and they seem more real than his recollections of everyday events. When he closes his eyes at night, the sounds of shattering glass and panicked voices resurface with vivid clarity, transporting him back to that fateful evening. His mind tells him it's over, but his body responds as if the threat is still present. Asher blames himself for not intervening sooner. He can't shake off the guilt that has taken up residence in his chest, a constant reminder of what he perceives as his own inadequacy. "I was just standing there," he tells himself, replaying the events over and over. His wife, Rachel, tries to reassure him that it wasn't his fault, but Asher can't seem to forgive himself. Ever since the bombing, Asher has become increasingly wary of those around him. He finds it difficult to trust anyone new, always wondering if they might be hiding something behind their friendly facade. As a prosecutor, he's accustomed to reading people, but now this skill has morphed into a source of anxiety. In meetings and court sessions, he catches himself scrutinizing colleagues and witnesses, searching for potential deception. Exhaustion has also become Asher's constant companion. He pushes through long hours at the office, often working late nights to prepare for upcoming trials. Despite his best efforts, fatigue seems to seep into every pore of his body. Even a brief power nap during lunch can trigger memories of that night - the feeling of being disoriented and helpless. Two specific smells have become potent triggers: the smell of smoke from fireplaces or candles, which instantly transports him back to the explosion, and the pungent aroma of cheap perfume, reminiscent of the restaurant's bathroom where he helped a survivor. Asher avoids social gatherings whenever possible, knowing that these smells might be lurking around every corner. Certain sounds also send Asher into high alert - firework explosions during holidays or car alarms outside his office window can make him jump out of his seat. These reactions are becoming increasingly difficult to conceal from colleagues and friends. Asher's relationships have begun to suffer as well. Rachel has expressed concern about the toll his exhaustion is taking on their relationship, but Asher feels like he's just trying to stay afloat. At work, colleagues have started noticing his short fuse and irritability during meetings. A few months ago, Asher snapped at a junior prosecutor during a heated discussion, causing an uncomfortable silence in the room. As the weight of these accumulated symptoms becomes unbearable, Asher has finally begun to realize that he can't keep going on like this. It's not just his relationships or job performance that are suffering; it's the quiet moments when he's alone with his thoughts that have become almost too much to bear. He's starting to wonder if he'll ever be able to silence the voice in his head, the one that keeps reminding him of what happened and how he failed. Asher is seeking help now because he fears losing himself entirely. As he sits in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands, he looks like a man who has lost control of his own story. The question that haunts him most - Will I ever be able to forgive myself? - lingers in the air, waiting for an answer that only therapy can provide.
